entries.lesson_title: Convolution of Two Equal-Width Rectangular Pulses
entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the continuous-time convolution of two equal-width rectangular pulses by tracking the moving overlap interval and converting its length into the resulting piecewise triangular waveform.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Convolution of Two Equal-Width Rectangular Pulses
sections.learning_goal: Recognize that convolving two equal-width rectangular pulses reduces to tracking a sliding overlap length and scaling that length by the pulse heights.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show two equal-width rectangular pulses on a tau-axis: a fixed support for x(tau), a flipped-and-shifted support for h(t - tau), and the overlap interval that changes as t increases.
visual_elements: labels for width T and time shift t
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use a clean signal-plot style with no decorative elements; emphasize supports and overlap rather than amplitude detail.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the base schema for equal-width rectangular-pulse convolution: the integral is determined by where the two supports overlap in the convolution variable.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Two equal-width rectangular pulses of width T, with x(tau) fixed on 0 <= tau <= T and h(t - tau) sliding across it as t changes.
paragraph_plan: Introduce the convolution integral and identify tau as the variable used to compare the fixed pulse with the shifted pulse.
Explain that the rectangular pulses are constant on their supports, so the integrand is nonzero only on the overlap of those supports.
Name the three structural events for equal widths: first contact, peak alignment, and last contact.
Preview the output shape: the overlap length rises linearly, then falls linearly, producing a triangular convolution output.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the tutorial compact: define the geometric overlap interpretation before any piecewise computation.

sections.section_title: Locating First Contact, Peak Alignment, and Last Contact
sections.learning_goal: Identify the key time breakpoints that divide the convolution into no-overlap, rising-overlap, peak, falling-overlap, and no-overlap regions.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show equal-width rectangular supports on a tau-axis at first contact, peak alignment, and last contact, with t values marked for a width-T pair.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Practice images should vary the pulse width or support location while preserving equal widths and clear edge labels.

question_policy.answer_format: An ordered list of the first-contact, peak-alignment, and last-contact t values.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Two unit-height rectangular pulses have equal width 4 and are positioned so x(tau) is fixed on 0 <= tau <= 4 while h(t - tau) slides across it. Which ordered triple gives first contact, peak alignment, and last contact?
distractor_plan: Use triples that shift all breakpoints by one pulse width.
Swap first contact and last contact.
Use half-width values instead of full-width values.
Omit the peak-alignment breakpoint.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For unit-height rectangular pulses x(tau) = 1 on 0 <= tau <= T and h(tau) = 1 on 0 <= tau <= T, locate first contact, peak alignment, and last contact for h(t - tau) as t varies.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Determine the breakpoints t = 0, t = T, and t = 2T that organize the equal-width rectangular-pulse convolution.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first worked example, isolating the contact times before any overlap-length computation.
solution_step_plan: Write the fixed support of x(tau) as [0, T].
Write the shifted support of h(t - tau) as [t - T, t].
Find when the shifted support first touches the fixed support.
Find when the two equal-width supports are fully aligned.
Find when the shifted support leaves the fixed support.
List the resulting time regions in order.
practice_variation_axes: whether the graph labels endpoints or width

sections.handoff_notes: The worked example should make the edge-tracking logic explicit; do not compute the triangular formula yet.

sections.section_title: Computing the Rising Overlap Length
sections.learning_goal: Compute the overlap length on the rising interval where the shifted rectangle is entering the fixed rectangle.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show the fixed support [0, T] and the shifted support [t - T, t] during the rising-overlap region 0 <= t <= T, with the overlap interval [0, t] shaded.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use a single-panel signal/support diagram; the image should support reading the interval endpoints, not solve the algebra.

question_policy.answer_format: A formula for the rising overlap length as a function of t.
question_policy.practice_question_model: For two equal-width rectangular pulses of width 5 with x(tau) fixed on 0 <= tau <= 5 and h(t - tau) supported on [t - 5, t], what is the overlap length for 0 <= t <= 5?
distractor_plan: Use the falling-region expression 10 - t.
Use the constant full width 5.
Use the shifted left endpoint t - 5 as the length.
Use zero by confusing partial overlap with no overlap.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For two unit-height rectangular pulses supported on [0, T], compute the overlap length for 0 <= t <= T.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the rising overlap length is L(t) = t.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This extends breakpoint identification by computing the length in the first active region.
solution_step_plan: State the fixed support [0, T] and shifted support [t - T, t].
Restrict to the rising interval 0 <= t <= T.
Identify the overlap interval as [0, t].
Subtract endpoints to get L(t) = t - 0.
Interpret the linear increase as the entering edge sweeping across the fixed pulse.
practice_variation_axes: support interval shifted away from the origin

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the worked example narrowly focused on length; amplitude scaling comes later.

sections.section_title: Computing the Falling Overlap Length
sections.learning_goal: Compute the overlap length on the falling interval where the shifted rectangle is leaving the fixed rectangle.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show the fixed support [0, T] and shifted support [t - T, t] during T <= t <= 2T, with the overlap interval [t - T, T] shaded.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use visual alignment that contrasts with the rising-overlap diagram so learners see which endpoint now moves inside the fixed support.

question_policy.answer_format: A formula for the falling overlap length as a function of t.
question_policy.practice_question_model: For two equal-width rectangular pulses of width 5 with x(tau) fixed on 0 <= tau <= 5 and h(t - tau) supported on [t - 5, t], what is the overlap length for 5 <= t <= 10?
distractor_plan: Use the rising-region expression t.
Use the constant full width 5.
Use T - t instead of 2T - t.
Use the no-overlap value 0 inside the active falling region.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For two unit-height rectangular pulses supported on [0, T], compute the overlap length for T <= t <= 2T.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the falling overlap length is L(t) = 2T - t.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This mirrors the rising-region computation, but the active overlap now shrinks as the shifted pulse exits.
solution_step_plan: State the fixed support [0, T] and shifted support [t - T, t].
Restrict to the falling interval T <= t <= 2T.
Identify the overlap interval as [t - T, T].
Subtract endpoints to get L(t) = T - (t - T).
Simplify to L(t) = 2T - t and check that it falls from T to 0.
practice_variation_axes: endpoint labels shown on the signal plot

sections.handoff_notes: Emphasize endpoint subtraction and boundary checks to prevent using the rising formula in the falling region.

sections.section_title: Scaling the Overlap Length by Rectangular Pulse Heights
sections.learning_goal: Convert overlap length into convolution value by multiplying by the product of the rectangular pulse heights.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show two equal-width rectangular pulses with labeled heights A and B and a shaded overlap interval of length L(t), with the constant product AB marked over the overlap.
visual_elements: label AB on the integrand over the overlap
image_policy.image_generation_notes: The visual should make clear that height scaling affects vertical amplitude while overlap length still controls the time dependence.

question_policy.answer_format: A scaled convolution expression for a specified active region.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Two equal-width rectangular pulses have width 5, heights 2 and 3, and supports arranged as in the standard equal-width case. Which expression gives y(t) on 0 <= t <= 5?
distractor_plan: Use the overlap length without multiplying by both heights.
Multiply by only one pulse height.
Use the falling-region length with the correct height product.
Use the width as a constant output over the rising region.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: If x(t) has height A and h(t) has height B, and both pulses have width T, compute the convolution value from the overlap length on the rising and falling regions.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that y(t) = ABt for 0 <= t <= T and y(t) = AB(2T - t) for T <= t <= 2T.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This adds amplitude scaling to the overlap-length formulas developed in the rising and falling regions.
solution_step_plan: State that x(tau)h(t - tau) equals AB wherever the supports overlap.
Use y(t) = AB L(t) because the integrand is constant over the overlap interval.
Substitute L(t) = t on the rising region.
Substitute L(t) = 2T - t on the falling region.
Check that the peak value is ABT at full alignment.

sections.handoff_notes: Do not let this section become a full piecewise assembly; its job is the height-product scaling rule.

sections.section_title: Writing the Piecewise Triangular Convolution Output
sections.learning_goal: Assemble the contact times, overlap lengths, and height scaling into the complete piecewise triangular convolution output.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show the final triangular output y(t) under the corresponding equal-width rectangular input pulses, with breakpoints 0, T, and 2T labeled and peak height ABT labeled.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: For practice, vary width and heights while keeping equal-width rectangles; the image should provide the signal data, not answer-choice diagrams.

question_policy.answer_format: A complete piecewise formula for y(t), including zero outside the active interval.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Two equal-width rectangular pulses have width 4, heights 2 and 1, and the standard supports that produce first contact at t = 0 and last contact at t = 8. Which piecewise expression gives y(t)?
distractor_plan: Use correct formulas but wrong breakpoints.
Omit the zero-output regions.
Use the unscaled overlap lengths instead of height-scaled values.
Use the rising expression on both active intervals.
Give the correct triangular shape with an incorrect peak height.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Write the complete convolution y(t) for two equal-width rectangular pulses of heights A and B supported on intervals of width T.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Produce the full triangular piecewise output with zero regions, rising region, falling region, and peak value.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This combines the earlier breakpoints, overlap-length formulas, and height scaling into one final output.
solution_step_plan: List the time regions t < 0, 0 <= t <= T, T <= t <= 2T, and t > 2T.
Assign y(t) = 0 in the no-overlap regions.
Use y(t) = ABt on the rising region.
Use y(t) = AB(2T - t) on the falling region.
State the peak value y(T) = ABT and connect the formula to the triangular waveform.
practice_variation_axes: support shifted away from the origin while preserving equal widths

sections.handoff_notes: This is the synthesis section; the writer should explicitly tie each piece of the formula to its overlap region.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the convolution of unequal-width rectangular pulses by identifying the edge-aligned breakpoints, expressing the sliding overlap length piecewise, and scaling by the pulse amplitudes to obtain the trapezoidal output.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Convolution of Unequal-Width Rectangular Pulses
sections.learning_goal: Introduce why unequal-width rectangular pulses produce a trapezoidal convolution output and preview the workflow of breakpoints, overlap length, and amplitude scaling.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Concept diagram showing a shorter rectangular pulse sliding across a wider rectangular pulse on the tau-axis, with first contact, full-overlap plateau, and last contact positions marked.
visual_elements: two rectangular pulses of different widths
first contact, full-overlap, and last-contact positions
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use the image to reduce load in the opening explanation; keep labels generic and avoid decorative styling.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Make explicit that unequal widths create three nonzero overlap behaviors: growing overlap, full overlap at the shorter width, and shrinking overlap.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use two positive rectangular pulses with unit heights and unequal widths, with the shorter pulse sliding across the longer pulse.
paragraph_plan: State the convolution-as-overlap-area viewpoint for rectangular pulses.
Define the edge-aligned breakpoints that split t into no-overlap, growing-overlap, full-overlap, shrinking-overlap, and no-overlap regions.
Explain that the shorter width determines the plateau overlap length.
Explain that pulse amplitudes scale the overlap area after the overlap length is found.
Preview the final trapezoidal output as a piecewise function built from the three nonzero overlap regions.
display_math_plan: Show y(t)=A_xA_hL(t), where L(t) is the overlap length of the two rectangular supports.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this section conceptual and compact; do not compute a full piecewise convolution before the example sections.

sections.section_title: Identifying Edge-Aligned Breakpoints
sections.learning_goal: Locate the ordered t-values where the shifted pulse first touches, becomes fully overlapping, stops being fully overlapping, and finally stops overlapping the fixed pulse.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Signal plot pair for x(tau) and h(t-tau) with unequal rectangular widths, showing the four edge-alignment events that determine the breakpoints.
visual_elements: left and right edges of both supports
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use simple horizontal rectangular supports on a tau-axis; vary widths in questions while preserving one shorter and one longer pulse.

question_policy.answer_format: ordered list of breakpoint t-values
question_policy.practice_question_model: From the signal plots for x(t) and h(t), where x(t) is nonzero on [0,3] and h(t) is nonzero on [0,8], list the edge-aligned breakpoints for the convolution.
distractor_plan: Check for omitted plateau-start or plateau-end breakpoints.
Check for using only the total support endpoints.
Check for adding widths in the wrong order when locating final contact.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For x(t)=2 on 0\le t\le 4 and h(t)=3 on 0\le t\le 7, identify the edge-aligned breakpoints of y(t)=x(t)*h(t).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Find the ordered breakpoints t=0, t=4, t=7, and t=11 before computing any overlap formulas.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from conceptual overlap regions to the first executable task: locating the t-values that control every later piece.
solution_step_plan: Write the fixed support of x(tau) as 0\le \tau\le 4.
Write the shifted support of h(t-\tau) as t-7\le \tau\le t.
Set the right edge of h(t-\tau) equal to the left edge of x(tau) for first contact.
Set the right edge of h(t-\tau) equal to the right edge of x(tau) for the start of full overlap.
Set the left edge of h(t-\tau) equal to the left edge of x(tau) for the end of full overlap.
Set the left edge of h(t-\tau) equal to the right edge of x(tau) for last contact.
practice_variation_axes: whether x or h is the shorter pulse
support starting point if still kept simple

sections.handoff_notes: Treat breakpoint identification as the control structure for the lesson; avoid computing overlap lengths in this section.

sections.section_title: Computing the Growing-Overlap Region
sections.learning_goal: Compute the rising branch by expressing the overlap length during first contact through full containment and multiplying by the amplitude product.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Rectangular pulse overlap diagram focused on the growing-overlap interval, with the overlap length increasing from zero to the shorter width.
visual_elements: wider shifted rectangular support entering from the left
breakpoint interval for the rising branch
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Show only the visual information needed to identify the growing overlap length; question images should vary widths and heights.

question_policy.answer_format: formula for y(t) on the growing-overlap interval
question_policy.practice_question_model: Using the plotted rectangular pulses with x(t)=2 on [0,3] and h(t)=5 on [0,8], find y(t) on the growing-overlap interval 0\le t\le 3.
distractor_plan: Check for giving overlap length without multiplying by amplitudes.
Check for using the longer width as the rising-branch endpoint.
Check for writing a constant plateau value instead of a linear function of t.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For x(t)=2 on 0\le t\le 4 and h(t)=3 on 0\le t\le 7, compute y(t) on the growing-overlap interval 0\le t\le 4.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the growing overlap length is L(t)=t and therefore y(t)=6t on 0\le t\le 4.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Uses the first two breakpoints from the prior section and adds the first overlap-length formula.
solution_step_plan: State that the relevant interval is from first contact to the start of full overlap.
Identify the overlap interval in tau as 0\le \tau\le t.
Compute the overlap length L(t)=t.
Multiply L(t) by the amplitude product 2\cdot 3.
Attach the correct t-interval to the resulting branch.
practice_variation_axes: whether the rising branch starts at t=0 or a shifted first-contact time

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the worked solution focused on the growing region only; later sections handle plateau, shrinking, and full assembly.

sections.section_title: Computing the Full-Overlap Plateau
sections.learning_goal: Compute the constant middle branch by recognizing that the shorter pulse is fully contained in the longer pulse throughout the plateau interval.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Rectangular pulse overlap diagram focused on the full-overlap plateau, with the entire shorter support contained inside the longer shifted support.
visual_elements: longer rectangular support extending beyond both edges
constant overlap length equal to shorter width
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Make containment visually clear; avoid unnecessary animation or extra regions.

question_policy.answer_format: constant formula for y(t) with its plateau interval
question_policy.practice_question_model: Using the plotted rectangular pulses with x(t)=2 on [0,3] and h(t)=5 on [0,8], find y(t) on the full-overlap plateau interval.
distractor_plan: Check for using the longer width instead of the shorter width as the overlap length.
Check for forgetting to multiply by both amplitudes.
Check for assigning the plateau to the entire output support.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For x(t)=2 on 0\le t\le 4 and h(t)=3 on 0\le t\le 7, compute y(t) on the full-overlap interval 4\le t\le 7.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the plateau overlap length is L(t)=4 and therefore y(t)=24 on 4\le t\le 7.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Extends the rising-branch computation to the constant middle case where overlap length stops changing.
solution_step_plan: State that the full-overlap interval runs from t=4 to t=7.
Recognize that the whole shorter support is covered throughout this interval.
Set the overlap length equal to the shorter width, L(t)=4.
Multiply by the amplitude product 2\cdot 3.
Attach the plateau interval to the constant branch.
practice_variation_axes: which signal has the shorter support

sections.handoff_notes: Emphasize the recognition move: full containment means constant overlap length, not a new integral setup.

sections.section_title: Computing the Shrinking-Overlap Region
sections.learning_goal: Compute the falling branch by expressing the overlap length after full containment ends and scaling it by the amplitude product.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Rectangular pulse overlap diagram focused on the shrinking-overlap interval, with overlap length decreasing from the shorter width to zero.
visual_elements: shifted rectangular support exiting to the right
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Show the exit-side edge alignment clearly so the expression total-width-minus-t is visually motivated.

question_policy.answer_format: formula for y(t) on the shrinking-overlap interval
question_policy.practice_question_model: Using the plotted rectangular pulses with x(t)=2 on [0,3] and h(t)=5 on [0,8], find y(t) on the shrinking-overlap interval 8\le t\le 11.
distractor_plan: Check for writing the rising expression again instead of a decreasing expression.
Check for using the wrong final-contact time in the expression.
Check for omitting amplitude scaling.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For x(t)=2 on 0\le t\le 4 and h(t)=3 on 0\le t\le 7, compute y(t) on the shrinking-overlap interval 7\le t\le 11.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the shrinking overlap length is L(t)=11-t and therefore y(t)=6(11-t) on 7\le t\le 11.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds the symmetric exit-side computation after the plateau, with overlap length decreasing instead of increasing or staying constant.
solution_step_plan: State that the shrinking interval runs from the end of full overlap to last contact.
Identify the overlap interval in tau as t-7\le \tau\le 4.
Compute the overlap length L(t)=4-(t-7)=11-t.
Multiply L(t) by the amplitude product 2\cdot 3.
Attach the correct t-interval to the falling branch.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the endpoint subtraction explicit so the writer prevents sign errors in the falling branch.

sections.section_title: Computing the Falling Overlap Area
sections.learning_goal: Compute the falling branch of the triangular convolution output by turning the shrinking overlap interval into a linearly decreasing area.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show the falling-region overlap for x(\tau) on [0, 2] and h(t-\tau) on [t-2, t] when 2\le t\le 4, with the overlap interval [t-2, 2] shaded and labeled.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Make the left endpoint of the overlap move with t and the right endpoint fixed at the end of x(\tau); keep labels uncluttered.

question_policy.answer_format: linear expression for y(t) on the falling interval
question_policy.practice_question_model: Let x(\tau)=3 on [0, 4] and h(\tau)=2 on [0, 4]. Find (x*h)(t) on the falling interval 4\le t\le 8.
distractor_plan: For feedback, watch for using t-W instead of 2W-t as the falling overlap length.
For feedback, watch for forgetting to multiply by both pulse heights.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For x(\tau)=2 on 0\le \tau\le 2 and h(\tau)=3 on 0\le \tau\le 2, find (x*h)(t) on the falling region 2\le t\le 4.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Derive y(t)=6(4-t) on the falling interval by multiplying the shrinking overlap length by the height product.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Uses the same pulses as the rising-area section but changes the overlap interval from growing to shrinking.
solution_step_plan: State the falling interval: 2\le t\le 4.
Write the supports x(\tau): [0, 2] and h(t-\tau): [t-2, t].
Identify the overlap interval during the falling region as [t-2, 2].
Compute the overlap length as 2-(t-2)=4-t.
Multiply the overlap length by the product of pulse heights, 2\cdot 3.
State the falling branch expression for y(t).
practice_variation_axes: ask for the falling interval explicitly or require it from endpoints

sections.handoff_notes: Contrast the falling interval with the rising interval so the learner sees why the expression decreases as t increases.

sections.section_title: Writing the Complete Piecewise Triangular Output
sections.learning_goal: Assemble the no-overlap, rising-area, and falling-area cases into one complete piecewise triangular convolution output.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show the input rectangular pulses with contact breakpoints and the completed triangular output y(t), with the rising and falling branches aligned to their time intervals.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use the image to support assembly of the final piecewise rule; do not make answer choices graphical.

question_policy.answer_format: complete piecewise definition of y(t)
question_policy.practice_question_model: Let x(\tau)=1 on [0, 3] and h(\tau)=5 on [0, 3]. Write the complete piecewise formula for (x*h)(t).
distractor_plan: For feedback, watch for omitting the zero-output regions outside the contact interval.
For feedback, watch for using the same expression on both the rising and falling intervals.
For feedback, watch for incorrect endpoint ordering in the piecewise definition.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For x(\tau)=2 on 0\le \tau\le 2 and h(\tau)=3 on 0\le \tau\le 2, write the complete piecewise formula for (x*h)(t).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Combine the breakpoints, zero-output regions, rising branch, and falling branch into the full triangular output.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Combines the prior region, rising-area, and falling-area work into the final lesson target.
solution_step_plan: List the breakpoints t=0, t=2, and t=4.
Write y(t)=0 for t<0 and for t>4.
Use the rising branch y(t)=6t for 0\le t\le 2.
Use the falling branch y(t)=6(4-t) for 2\le t\le 4.
Assemble the cases in increasing order of t.
Check that the two nonzero branches meet at the peak value when t=2.
practice_variation_axes: shift supports while keeping equal widths
include or omit an output sketch as supporting data

sections.handoff_notes: This is the synthesis section; the example writer should make the continuity/peak check brief and keep the main focus on assembling the piecewise output.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute trapezoidal outputs from unequal-width rectangular-pulse convolution by partitioning time into no-overlap, growing-overlap, full-overlap, and shrinking-overlap regions.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Trapezoidal Outputs from Rectangular Pulses
sections.learning_goal: Recognize that convolving unequal-width rectangular pulses produces a trapezoid because the overlap length grows, stays constant, and then shrinks.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show two unit-height rectangular pulses of unequal widths on aligned time axes, a sliding overlap snapshot in the convolution variable, and the resulting trapezoidal output divided into no-overlap, growing-overlap, full-overlap, and shrinking-overlap regions.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use clean signal plots with labeled breakpoints and region names; avoid decorative styling and avoid adding unrelated signal shapes.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Explain how unequal rectangular pulse widths create a trapezoidal convolution output from overlap length.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use unit-height pulses with supports [0, 5] and [0, 2] so the shorter pulse can fully overlap the longer pulse.
paragraph_plan: State that the convolution value is the area of overlap between x(tau) and h(t - tau) when the pulses have unit height.
Contrast equal-width pulses, where the overlap immediately changes from growing to shrinking, with unequal-width pulses, where the shorter pulse can be fully inside the longer pulse.
Name the four interior regions in order: growing overlap, full overlap, and shrinking overlap, with no-overlap regions before first contact and after last contact.
Connect each region to the output shape: zero, increasing ramp, constant plateau, decreasing ramp, zero.
Preview that the lesson will compute each piece by ordering breakpoints and writing the overlap length on each interval.
display_math_plan: For unit-height rectangular pulses, y(t) = overlap length.
Region pattern: 0, growing ramp, plateau, shrinking ramp, 0

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: not-applicable
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: not-applicable
example_outline.variation_from_previous: not-applicable

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the tutorial to a minimum effective dose; the visual should reduce cognitive load by making the region names refer to visible overlap behavior.

sections.section_title: Ordering the Breakpoints for Unequal-Width Rectangular Pulses
sections.learning_goal: Order the contact times that divide unequal rectangular-pulse convolution into no-overlap, growing-overlap, full-overlap, shrinking-overlap, and no-overlap regions.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show x(tau) with support [0, 5] and h(t - tau) sweeping across it for a pulse h of width 2; mark the breakpoints t = 0, 2, 5, and 7 on a shared t-axis.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: For questions, vary the long and short pulse widths but keep axis labels and breakpoint markers clear; do not include answer text in the image.

question_policy.answer_format: ordered breakpoints with interval labels
question_policy.practice_question_model: For unit-height rectangular pulses x(t) = 1 on 0 <= t <= 6 and h(t) = 1 on 0 <= t <= 3, list the ordered breakpoints and name the region between each consecutive pair.
distractor_plan: Flag responses that swap the short width and long width breakpoints.
Flag responses that omit the sum-of-widths breakpoint.
Flag responses that label the middle interval as growing or shrinking instead of full-overlap.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For unit-height rectangular pulses x(t) = 1 on 0 <= t <= 5 and h(t) = 1 on 0 <= t <= 2, list the convolution breakpoints that separate the no-overlap, growing-overlap, full-overlap, shrinking-overlap, and no-overlap regions.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Produce the ordered breakpoints t = 0, 2, 5, 7 and attach the correct region label to each interval.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Move from qualitative trapezoid recognition to concrete breakpoint ordering for one unequal-width pulse pair.
solution_step_plan: Identify the longer support length and the shorter support length.
Use first contact at t = 0 and last contact at t = 5 + 2.
Use the shorter width to mark the end of the growing-overlap interval.
Use the longer width to mark the end of the full-overlap interval.
Write the ordered region map from left to right.
practice_variation_axes: whether x or h is the shorter pulse
support endpoints that still begin at zero

sections.handoff_notes: Keep endpoint conventions informal; in continuous-time area calculations, isolated endpoint inclusions do not change the convolution value.

sections.section_title: Identifying No-Overlap Regions Before and After Contact
sections.learning_goal: Determine the time intervals where the rectangular pulses do not overlap, so the convolution output is zero.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show the same unequal-width pulse pair with h(t - tau) positioned entirely before first contact and entirely after last contact; highlight that the overlap length is zero in both outer regions.
visual_elements: zero output on the y(t) axis
image_policy.image_generation_notes: For question images, vary pulse widths while making the first-contact and last-contact positions visually unambiguous.

question_policy.answer_format: two no-overlap intervals and the value y(t) = 0
question_policy.practice_question_model: For unit-height rectangular pulses x(t) = 1 on 0 <= t <= 6 and h(t) = 1 on 0 <= t <= 3, identify the time intervals before first contact and after last contact where y(t) = 0.
distractor_plan: Flag responses that use the shorter width as the last-contact time.
Flag responses that include the full-overlap interval as a no-overlap region.
Flag responses that give a nonzero output outside the contact interval.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For unit-height rectangular pulses x(t) = 1 on 0 <= t <= 5 and h(t) = 1 on 0 <= t <= 2, identify the time intervals where the convolution output is zero because the pulses do not overlap.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Conclude that y(t) = 0 before first contact and after last contact, using t < 0 and t > 7 as the outer regions.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Use the ordered breakpoints from the prior section to isolate only the two outer no-overlap regions.
solution_step_plan: Recall the ordered breakpoints t = 0, 2, 5, 7.
Identify t < 0 as the region before first contact.
Identify t > 7 as the region after last contact.
State that the overlap length is zero in both regions.
Write the corresponding output value y(t) = 0.
practice_variation_axes: strict versus non-strict endpoint notation handled consistently

sections.handoff_notes: Do not let the section become a full piecewise assembly; keep the active move focused on zero-output regions.

sections.section_title: Computing the Growing-Overlap Ramp
sections.learning_goal: Compute the increasing ramp by expressing the growing overlap length as a function of time.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show the growing-overlap interval for x(tau) on [0, 5] and a width-2 h(t - tau), with the overlap segment labeled as length t for 0 < t < 2.
visual_elements: moving rectangular support during first contact
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Question images should vary the pulse widths but keep the growing-overlap segment explicitly visible as a length measured from first contact.

question_policy.answer_format: formula for y(t) on the growing-overlap interval
question_policy.practice_question_model: For unit-height rectangular pulses x(t) = 1 on 0 <= t <= 6 and h(t) = 1 on 0 <= t <= 3, compute y(t) on the growing-overlap interval.
distractor_plan: Flag responses that use the shorter pulse width as a constant plateau value during the growing interval.
Flag responses that write the shrinking expression on the growing interval.
Flag responses that omit the valid time interval for the ramp.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For unit-height rectangular pulses x(t) = 1 on 0 <= t <= 5 and h(t) = 1 on 0 <= t <= 2, compute y(t) on the growing-overlap region.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the overlap length is t on 0 < t < 2, so the growing ramp is y(t) = t for unit-height pulses.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Move from identifying zero regions to computing the first nonzero region by measuring overlap length.
solution_step_plan: Use the breakpoint map to locate the growing-overlap interval 0 < t < 2.
Identify the left and right endpoints of the overlap segment in the tau variable.
Compute overlap length as right endpoint minus left endpoint.
Multiply by the unit heights to get the convolution value.
Write the ramp formula together with its interval.
practice_variation_axes: pulse height product if later variation includes amplitudes
interval notation for the growing region

sections.handoff_notes: Use subgoal labels around interval, overlap length, and output formula so the example writer does not collapse the reasoning into one algebra step.

sections.section_title: Computing the Full-Overlap Plateau
sections.learning_goal: Compute the constant plateau by recognizing when the shorter rectangular pulse is fully overlapped.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show the shorter pulse fully inside the longer pulse for x(tau) on [0, 5] and width-2 h(t - tau), with the overlap length fixed at 2 for 2 < t < 5.
visual_elements: shorter rectangle fully inside longer rectangle
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Make the full-overlap position visually distinct from partial overlap; for questions, vary widths while preserving a nonempty plateau.

question_policy.answer_format: constant value and interval for the plateau
question_policy.practice_question_model: For unit-height rectangular pulses x(t) = 1 on 0 <= t <= 6 and h(t) = 1 on 0 <= t <= 3, compute y(t) on the full-overlap plateau interval.
distractor_plan: Flag responses that use the longer pulse width as the plateau height.
Flag responses that keep y(t) variable instead of constant on the plateau.
Flag responses that place the plateau outside the interval from shorter width to longer width.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For unit-height rectangular pulses x(t) = 1 on 0 <= t <= 5 and h(t) = 1 on 0 <= t <= 2, compute y(t) on the full-overlap plateau.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the overlap length stays equal to the shorter width, so y(t) = 2 on 2 < t < 5 for unit-height pulses.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Add the plateau case where overlap no longer changes with t because the shorter pulse is fully covered.
solution_step_plan: Use the breakpoint map to locate the full-overlap interval 2 < t < 5.
Recognize that the entire shorter pulse is inside the longer pulse.
Set the overlap length equal to the shorter pulse width.
Multiply by the unit heights to get the plateau value.
Write the constant formula together with its interval.

sections.handoff_notes: Emphasize that the plateau height comes from the shorter width, not from the duration of the longer pulse.

sections.section_title: Computing the Shrinking-Overlap Ramp
sections.learning_goal: Compute the decreasing ramp by expressing the shrinking overlap length as total contact width minus time.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show the shrinking-overlap interval for x(tau) on [0, 5] and a width-2 h(t - tau), with overlap length labeled 7 - t for 5 < t < 7.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Question images should make the last-contact breakpoint and remaining overlap length easy to read without adding symbolic clutter.

question_policy.answer_format: formula for y(t) on the shrinking-overlap interval
question_policy.practice_question_model: For unit-height rectangular pulses x(t) = 1 on 0 <= t <= 6 and h(t) = 1 on 0 <= t <= 3, compute y(t) on the shrinking-overlap interval.
distractor_plan: Flag responses that reuse the growing formula t on the shrinking interval.
Flag responses that use long width minus t instead of total contact width minus t.
Flag responses that omit the shrinking interval.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For unit-height rectangular pulses x(t) = 1 on 0 <= t <= 5 and h(t) = 1 on 0 <= t <= 2, compute y(t) on the shrinking-overlap region.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the overlap length is 7 - t on 5 < t < 7, so the shrinking ramp is y(t) = 7 - t for unit-height pulses.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Mirror the growing-ramp computation after the full-overlap plateau, using last contact to form the decreasing expression.
solution_step_plan: Use the breakpoint map to locate the shrinking-overlap interval 5 < t < 7.
Identify the last-contact time as the sum of the pulse widths.
Express the remaining overlap length as last-contact time minus t.
Multiply by the unit heights to get the convolution value.
Write the decreasing ramp formula together with its interval.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the worked example parallel to the growing-ramp section so the learner sees the symmetry without treating it as a new method.

sections.section_title: Assembling the Complete Trapezoidal Output
sections.learning_goal: Combine the zero regions, growing ramp, plateau, and shrinking ramp into one complete piecewise convolution output.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show the input rectangular pulses and the complete output trapezoid for x(t) on [0, 5] and h(t) on [0, 2], with breakpoints 0, 2, 5, and 7 aligned to the piecewise formula regions.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: For questions, vary pulse widths and display the corresponding input supports; do not render the final answer in the image.

question_policy.answer_format: complete piecewise formula for y(t)
question_policy.practice_question_model: For unit-height rectangular pulses x(t) = 1 on 0 <= t <= 6 and h(t) = 1 on 0 <= t <= 3, assemble the complete piecewise formula for y(t).
distractor_plan: Flag responses with missing zero-output regions.
Flag responses with breakpoints in the wrong order.
Flag responses with plateau height equal to the longer width instead of the shorter width.
Flag responses with shrinking ramp written using the wrong intercept.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For unit-height rectangular pulses x(t) = 1 on 0 <= t <= 5 and h(t) = 1 on 0 <= t <= 2, assemble the complete piecewise formula for the convolution output y(t).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Combine the previously computed pieces into a single trapezoidal piecewise output: zero, growing ramp, plateau, shrinking ramp, zero.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Synthesize all prior region computations into the complete output rather than computing only one region.
solution_step_plan: List the ordered breakpoints 0, 2, 5, 7.
Write y(t) = 0 on the two no-overlap regions.
Insert the growing-ramp formula on the first nonzero interval.
Insert the plateau value on the full-overlap interval.
Insert the shrinking-ramp formula on the final nonzero interval.
Check that adjacent pieces meet at the trapezoid height and return to zero at last contact.
practice_variation_axes: optional pulse-height scaling after the unit-height structure is stable

sections.handoff_notes: Treat this as assembly, not a new derivation; preserve the same simple pulse pair so the final section consolidates the lesson's core move.

entries.lesson_title: Geometric Area Methods for Rectangular Pulse Convolution
entries.lesson_core_move: Compute rectangular-pulse convolutions by translating overlap intervals into geometric areas that produce the correct triangular or trapezoidal piecewise output across time.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Geometric Area Methods for Rectangular Pulse Convolution
sections.learning_goal: Explain how the value of a rectangular-pulse convolution at a fixed time can be found as the geometric area of the overlap region in the tau-axis picture.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show x(tau) as a fixed rectangular pulse and h(t - tau) as a shifted rectangular pulse on the same tau axis, with their overlap shaded as a rectangle whose width is the overlap interval and whose height is the product of pulse amplitudes.
visual_elements: labels for overlap width and amplitude product
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use a clean signal plot, not a decorative graphic. Keep the visual focused on one fixed time value so the tutorial can introduce area before piecewise cases.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach that rectangular-pulse convolution can be evaluated by replacing the integral over the nonzero overlap with rectangle area: amplitude product times overlap length.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Two positive rectangular pulses overlap on a single interval of length L at one fixed time t, with constant pulse heights A and B.
paragraph_plan: State that earlier overlap mechanics determine where both factors are nonzero, and this lesson turns that overlap interval into area.
Introduce the fixed-time tau-axis picture: x(tau) stays fixed while h(t - tau) slides as t changes.
Explain that inside the overlap, the integrand is constant for rectangular pulses, so the integral is the area of a rectangle.
Name the two geometric ingredients: overlap length and height product.
Preview the three possible area behaviors across t: growing, constant full overlap, and shrinking.
display_math_plan: y(t) = integral x(tau) h(t - tau) d tau
For rectangular pulses on an overlap of length L(t), y(t) = A B L(t).

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the tutorial compact. Do not derive a full convolution yet; establish the area schema that the later examples will repeatedly use.

sections.section_title: Converting an Overlap Interval into Rectangular Area
sections.learning_goal: Convert a known overlap interval and two rectangular-pulse amplitudes into the convolution value at one fixed time.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show two rectangular pulse factors on a tau axis at one fixed time, with the overlapping interval shaded and endpoint labels that make the width visible.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Question images should vary the overlap endpoints and pulse heights while preserving the single-interval rectangle-area task.

question_policy.answer_format: numeric area value or simplified product
question_policy.practice_question_model: At a fixed time, the graph shows x(tau) = 2 and h(t - tau) = 3 over their common nonzero interval 1 <= tau <= 4. Use geometric area to find y(t).
distractor_plan: For validation, watch for using endpoint sum instead of interval width.
For validation, watch for using one pulse height instead of the amplitude product.
For validation, watch for integrating over the union instead of the overlap.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: At a fixed time, x(tau) has height 2, h(t - tau) has height 3, and the two pulses overlap only on 1 <= tau <= 4. Use the geometric area method to find the convolution value y(t) at that time.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the convolution value is the rectangle area formed by width 4 - 1 and height product 2 times 3.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first active step after the tutorial: the overlap interval is already known, so the only new action is converting width and amplitudes into area.
solution_step_plan: Identify the overlap width from the interval endpoints.
Identify the constant integrand height as the product of the two pulse amplitudes.
Multiply width by height product to get the area.
State the result as the convolution value at the fixed time.
practice_variation_axes: include a left endpoint that is negative while keeping positive width

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this section to one fixed-time area computation. Do not introduce growing, shrinking, or piecewise time intervals yet.

sections.section_title: Finding Growing and Shrinking Areas for a Triangular Output
sections.learning_goal: Use changing overlap length to produce the increasing and decreasing pieces of a triangular rectangular-pulse convolution.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show a sequence of tau-axis overlap snapshots for equal-width rectangular pulses: first contact, growing partial overlap, full alignment at the peak, shrinking partial overlap, and separation.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use minimal snapshot panels or a compact annotated signal diagram. The visual should support recognition of the two linear overlap lengths that form the triangle.

question_policy.answer_format: piecewise expression for the nonzero triangular output
question_policy.practice_question_model: Two unit-height rectangular pulses are supported on 0 <= tau <= 3 and 0 <= t - tau <= 3. Use growing and shrinking overlap areas to write y(t) for the nonzero time interval.
distractor_plan: For validation, watch for reversing the growing and shrinking formulas.
For validation, watch for using the support width as a constant plateau.
For validation, watch for missing the final endpoint of the nonzero interval.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Two unit-height rectangular pulses each have width 2. Use geometric area to find the triangular convolution output over the times when the pulses overlap.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Demonstrate that the overlap area grows linearly until full alignment and then shrinks linearly until separation, producing a triangular output.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Instead of one fixed overlap interval, the overlap width now changes with t in two linear cases.
solution_step_plan: Identify the first contact time, peak full-alignment time, and final separation time.
Write the growing overlap length on the first interval.
Write the shrinking overlap length on the second interval.
Multiply by the unit amplitude product.
Assemble the two nonzero pieces and note that the output is zero outside them.
practice_variation_axes: shift both supports while preserving equal widths
use unit heights so the focus remains on changing overlap length

sections.handoff_notes: The example should feel like a controlled extension of Section 2: area is still width times height, but width is now a function of t.

sections.section_title: Finding Constant Full-Overlap Area for a Trapezoidal Output
sections.learning_goal: Identify the growing, constant full-overlap, and shrinking area cases that create a trapezoidal rectangular-pulse convolution.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show overlap snapshots for unequal-width rectangular pulses where the shorter pulse first partially overlaps, then is fully inside the longer pulse, then partially overlaps again.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Make the shorter pulse visibly fit inside the longer pulse during the middle case so the constant-area plateau is visually unavoidable.

question_policy.answer_format: piecewise expression for the nonzero trapezoidal output
question_policy.practice_question_model: A unit-height rectangular pulse of width 5 is convolved with a unit-height rectangular pulse of width 2. Use geometric area cases to write the nonzero trapezoidal output y(t).
distractor_plan: For validation, watch for omitting the constant full-overlap interval.
For validation, watch for setting the plateau height to the longer width instead of the shorter width.
For validation, watch for placing the plateau endpoints at the wrong contact times.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A unit-height rectangular pulse of width 4 is convolved with a unit-height rectangular pulse of width 2. Use geometric area to find the trapezoidal output over the nonzero time interval.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show how unequal widths add a middle interval where the shorter pulse is fully overlapped and the area stays constant.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This adds the full-overlap plateau that does not occur for equal-width triangular outputs.
solution_step_plan: Identify the contact times that separate no overlap, growing partial overlap, full overlap, shrinking partial overlap, and no overlap.
Write the growing overlap length on the first nonzero interval.
Write the constant overlap length during full overlap as the shorter pulse width.
Write the shrinking overlap length on the final nonzero interval.
Assemble the three nonzero area pieces.
practice_variation_axes: swap which signal has the longer support while preserving the same geometry

sections.handoff_notes: Emphasize that the plateau comes from full overlap of the shorter rectangle, not from an algebraic shortcut.

sections.section_title: Applying Pulse Amplitudes to Geometric Area
sections.learning_goal: Scale the overlap-length geometry by the product of the rectangular pulse amplitudes.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show rectangular pulses with unequal height labels and a shaded overlap region, making clear that the geometric area uses overlap length times the product of the two heights.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Question images should vary both support widths and height labels. Avoid visual clutter by labeling only the endpoints needed for the area cases.

question_policy.answer_format: scaled area expression or scaled piecewise expression
question_policy.practice_question_model: The overlap length for two rectangular pulses is L(t) = t on 0 <= t <= 2 and L(t) = 4 - t on 2 <= t <= 4. If the pulse heights are 3 and 2, use geometric area to write y(t) on the nonzero intervals.
distractor_plan: For validation, watch for adding amplitudes instead of multiplying them.
For validation, watch for applying the amplitude product to only one piece.
For validation, watch for changing the overlap breakpoints when only amplitudes changed.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Two rectangular pulses have heights 2 and 3. Their overlap length is t for 0 <= t <= 2 and 4 - t for 2 <= t <= 4. Use geometric area to write the convolution output on the nonzero intervals.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that nonunit amplitudes do not change the overlap lengths but multiply every area piece by the amplitude product.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This keeps the triangular area structure but adds nonunit heights, separating geometric width from amplitude scaling.
solution_step_plan: Identify the existing overlap-length pieces.
Compute the amplitude product.
Multiply each overlap-length piece by the amplitude product.
Write the scaled nonzero output pieces without changing their time intervals.
practice_variation_axes: change the pair of pulse amplitudes
use a trapezoidal overlap-length function instead of a triangular one
include one fractional amplitude while keeping endpoints simple

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the conceptual emphasis on amplitude scaling after overlap geometry has been determined. Do not let this become a generic algebra simplification section.

sections.section_title: Assembling the Piecewise Convolution from Area Cases
sections.learning_goal: Combine no-overlap, partial-overlap, full-overlap, and amplitude-scaled area cases into one complete piecewise convolution output.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show the full set of overlap cases for two rectangular pulses across time, with breakpoints marked and shaded regions indicating each nonzero area case.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: The image should support assembling the final piecewise output. Keep each panel simple and align panels left-to-right in increasing t.

question_policy.answer_format: complete piecewise convolution including zero outside the support
question_policy.practice_question_model: Let x(tau) have height 2 on 0 <= tau <= 3 and let h(t - tau) have height 1 on 0 <= t - tau <= 1. Use geometric area cases to write the complete piecewise formula for y(t), including where it is zero.
distractor_plan: For validation, watch for excluding the zero-output intervals.
For validation, watch for mixing up the growing and shrinking endpoint formulas.
For validation, watch for leaving out the amplitude product in the final piecewise formula.
For validation, watch for inconsistent breakpoint inequalities.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Let x(tau) have height 2 on 0 <= tau <= 3, and let h(t - tau) have height 1 on 0 <= t - tau <= 1. Use geometric area cases to assemble the complete piecewise formula for y(t).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Demonstrate the full handoff from visual overlap cases to a complete piecewise convolution formula with correct breakpoints, zero intervals, and amplitude scaling.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This final section combines the earlier moves: interval width, growing and shrinking areas, full-overlap behavior when present, amplitude product, and zero outside overlap.
solution_step_plan: List the time breakpoints where the overlap case changes.
Assign the correct area formula to each nonzero interval.
Apply the pulse amplitude product to each area formula.
Add zero pieces before first contact and after final separation.
Write the final piecewise convolution in increasing time order.
practice_variation_axes: change support widths while keeping endpoints integer
